contents.title: Understanding Wafer-Capacity Prepayment – August 30, 2026
contents.body:
## Wafer-Capacity Prepayment – August 30, 2026

As of August 30, 2026, wafer-capacity prepayment arrangements are disclosed in filings by foundries, fabless semiconductor suppliers, and equipment vendors. This record compiles publicly available terms, counterparties, and dates. No analysis or projection is included.

## Foundry Prepayment Disclosures

TSMC disclosed in its 2025 annual report, filed March 2026, that customer prepayments for wafer capacity totaled NT$142.6 billion as of December 31, 2025, compared with NT$118.3 billion as of December 31, 2024. The filing states that these amounts are recorded as contract liabilities and are applied against future wafer shipments. The report lists no individual customer names.

Samsung Electronics disclosed in its 2025 business report, filed February 2026, that advance payments for foundry capacity were KRW 4.12 trillion as of December 31, 2025, down from KRW 4.87 trillion a year earlier. The report attributes the change to the timing of capacity reservations and shipment recognition.

GlobalFoundries disclosed in its Form 10-K for fiscal year 2025, filed February 2026, that customer prepayments and deferred revenue for wafer capacity were USD 1.34 billion as of December 31, 2025, compared with USD 1.21 billion as of December 31, 2024. The filing states that these balances relate to long-term supply agreements with durations of three to five years.

United Microelectronics Corporation disclosed in its 2025 annual report, filed March 2026, that advance receipts for wafer capacity were NT$28.7 billion as of December 31, 2025, compared with NT$31.2 billion as of December 31, 2024. The report states that the decrease reflects the completion of certain prepaid capacity contracts.

## Customer-Side Disclosures

Nvidia disclosed in its Form 10-Q for the quarter ended April 26, 2026, filed May 2026, that prepaid wafer capacity and related supply commitments were USD 3.21 billion as of April 26, 2026, compared with USD 2.74 billion as of January 25, 2026. The filing states that these amounts are included in prepaid expenses and other current assets and in other non-current assets.

AMD disclosed in its Form 10-Q for the quarter ended March 28, 2026, filed April 2026, that prepaid wafer capacity was USD 1.18 billion as of March 28, 2026, compared with USD 1.05 billion as of December 27, 2025. The filing states that the amounts relate to long-term wafer supply agreements.

Apple disclosed in its Form 10-Q for the quarter ended March 28, 2026, filed May 2026, that prepaid wafer capacity and related manufacturing commitments were USD 2.46 billion as of March 28, 2026, compared with USD 2.19 billion as of December 28, 2025. The filing states that these amounts are recorded within prepaid expenses and other current assets and other non-current assets.

Qualcomm disclosed in its Form 10-Q for the quarter ended March 29, 2026, filed April 2026, that prepaid wafer capacity was USD 0.94 billion as of March 29, 2026, compared with USD 0.88 billion as of December 28, 2025. The filing states that the amounts relate to supply agreements with multiple foundries.

Broadcom disclosed in its Form 10-Q for the quarter ended May 3, 2026, filed June 2026, that prepaid wafer capacity and related supply commitments were USD 1.07 billion as of May 3, 2026, compared with USD 0.99 billion as of February 1, 2026. The filing states that the amounts are recorded in prepaid expenses and other current assets.

## Equipment and Materials Prepayments

ASML disclosed in its 2025 annual report, filed February 2026, that customer prepayments for lithography systems and capacity reservations were EUR 4.31 billion as of December 31, 2025, compared with EUR 3.87 billion as of December 31, 2024. The report states that these amounts are recorded as contract liabilities.

Applied Materials disclosed in its Form 10-K for fiscal year 2025, filed December 2025, that customer prepayments and deferred revenue were USD 2.12 billion as of October 26, 2025, compared with USD 1.98 billion as of October 27, 2024. The filing states that these balances relate to long-term supply agreements.

Lam Research disclosed in its Form 10-K for fiscal year 2025, filed August 2025, that customer prepayments were USD 1.03 billion as of June 29, 2025, compared with USD 0.91 billion as of June 30, 2024. The filing states that the amounts relate to capacity reservations for etch and deposition equipment.

Tokyo Electron disclosed in its annual report for the fiscal year ended March 31, 2026, filed May 2026, that advance receipts for equipment were JPY 312.4 billion as of March 31, 2026, compared with JPY 287.6 billion as of March 31, 2025. The report states that the amounts are recorded as contract liabilities.

## Government and Central Bank Records

The Bank of Japan (BoJ) published its Tankan survey for June 2026 on July 1, 2026. The survey reports that large manufacturers in the electrical machinery sector reported a diffusion index of plus 12 for fixed investment, unchanged from the March 2026 survey. The survey does not separately report wafer-capacity prepayments.

The U.S. Department of Commerce published a notice in the Federal Register on April 15, 2026, regarding the CHIPS Incentives Program. The notice states that recipients of funding may use awards for capacity expansion and that prepayment arrangements with customers are permitted under the program's terms. The notice does not disclose individual prepayment amounts.

The European Commission published a report on March 10, 2026, regarding the European Chips Act. The report states that member states have committed EUR 43 billion in public funding for semiconductor capacity. The report does not separately report wafer-capacity prepayments.

## Contract Terms and Dates

Public filings describe typical prepayment terms. Durations range from one to five years. Amounts are recorded as contract liabilities by suppliers and as prepaid expenses by customers. Application against future shipments occurs as wafers are delivered. Refund provisions are described in some filings as contingent on capacity delivery schedules.

As of August 30, 2026, no single filing discloses all counterparties to a given prepayment arrangement. The most recent quarterly filings are for periods ending April 26, 2026, May 3, 2026, and March 31, 2026. Annual reports for fiscal years ended December 31, 2025, and March 31, 2026, are the most recent annual disclosures. All figures are as reported in the cited filings and are not adjusted for subsequent events.

contents.title: Kestrel Semiconductor advanced-packaging lead times in Malaysia: the dated series
contents.body:
I run procurement for a mid-size fabless shop, and I have spent most of 2026 staring at Kestrel Semiconductor's Penang advanced-packaging queue. Here is the blunt version: the queue has been shrinking, and it has been shrinking faster than anyone on the buy side expected. I have the dated numbers, and I have the week counts, because that is the only way to talk about this business without getting lied to.

## The Penang queue, dated

On 1 June 2026, Kestrel's Penang advanced-packaging lead time was 26 weeks. That was the number we built our H2 allocation plan around. It was ugly. It meant anything we booked in June landed in December, which meant our Q4 customer commitments were effectively locked before we had a single wafer out of the foundry. We were quoting our own customers at 30 weeks and padding the back end because we did not trust the 26.

By 1 August 2026, the same Penang line was quoting 22 weeks. That is a four-week improvement in eight weeks, which sounds modest until you annualise it. Then on 15 September 2026, the number came in at 18 weeks. So from 1 June 2026 to 15 September 2026, we went from 26 weeks to 18 weeks, a cut of 31%, while capacity grew from 11,000 units to 16,000 units a month. That is eight weeks of lead time gone in fifteen weeks of calendar time. I have been doing this for eleven years and I have never seen a packaging queue compress that fast without a demand shock behind it.

## What actually moved

The obvious explanation is capacity. Kestrel commissioned Phase 2 at Penang on 15 August 2026. That is the date I have from the supplier's own capacity notice, and it lines up with the 1 August 2026 quote of 22 weeks, because the line was already loading Phase 2 tools in late July. Phase 2 is the advanced-packaging expansion, the one they have been teasing since 2024. It is real, it is running, and it is the reason the queue is moving.

The less obvious explanation is mix. Kestrel has been quietly pushing lower-layer flip-chip work off Penang and onto its other back-end sites, which frees the Penang line for the high-layer-count stuff that actually pays. I do not have that in writing. I have it from three separate conversations with people who would know, and the behaviour of the quotes supports it. Our simple parts are suddenly quoting out of a different site. Our hard parts are still Penang, but they are quoting shorter.

## Johor is not the hedge it was

Here is the part that matters for anyone building a dual-source strategy. The Johor alternative, the one everyone has been treating as the safe fallback, was still at 24 weeks on 15 September 2026. Read that again. Penang is at 18 weeks. Johor is at 24 weeks. The fallback is now six weeks slower than the primary.

That is a complete inversion of where we were in the spring. Back in Q1, Johor was the fast lane and Penang was the queue you endured because you had no choice. Now the fast lane is Penang and Johor is the queue. If you are still splitting your volume 50/50 on the assumption that Johor is the safer bet, you are paying a six-week penalty for the privilege of being wrong.

I am not saying abandon Johor. I am saying reprice it. If your allocation model still treats Johor as the low-risk path, your model is stale. The risk premium has flipped.

## What I am doing with my own allocation

I moved our Q4 volume. Not all of it, but the majority. We had been running roughly 60/40 Penang/Johor since the spring, and I have pushed that to 80/20 as of the third week of September. The reason is simple arithmetic. At 18 weeks, Penang lands our Q4 build in the first half of January. At 24 weeks, Johor lands it in early March. One of those keeps our customer commitments. The other one does not.

The counterargument is concentration risk. If Penang sneezes, we are exposed. That is fair, and I am not pretending it is not. But concentration risk is a probability, and a six-week lead-time gap is a certainty. I will take the certain six weeks and manage the probability with buffer stock on the two parts where a Penang hiccup would actually hurt us.

The other thing I am doing is re-quoting everything. Every PO we have out with Kestrel, I have asked for a fresh lead time against the 15 September 2026 number. Some of them came back at 18 weeks. Some came back longer because of specific layer counts or specific substrate constraints. The headline number is not the number for your part. The headline number is the number for the easiest part on the line. Do not plan against the headline.

## The part nobody wants to say out loud

Kestrel is not doing this out of generosity. They are doing it because Phase 2 gave them capacity and because they want the high-layer-count volume, and the way you win high-layer-count volume is by being the fastest quote in the room. The 26 weeks to 18 weeks move is a commercial play as much as a capacity play. That is fine. I do not need my suppliers to be charitable. I need them to be predictable, and right now Penang is more predictable than it has been all year.

The question is whether it holds. Phase 2 is commissioned, but commissioning is not the same as mature yield. If the new line runs into a substrate problem in October, that 18 weeks goes back to 22 in a hurry. I have seen it happen. So I am treating the 18 weeks as real but not permanent. I am booking against it. I am not signing annual contracts against it.

If you are still quoting your own customers off a 26-week assumption, you are leaving weeks on the table. If you are still routing volume to Johor because it used to be the fast lane, you are paying for a memory. The numbers as of 15 September 2026 are 18 weeks Penang, 24 weeks Johor, and a Phase 2 line that came online on 15 August 2026. That is the whole picture. Act accordingly.

answers.conclusion: A Kestrel statement dated 2 September 2026 says Phase 2 reached its rated capacity on 28 August 2026. The statement gives no unit figures. A second statement dated 20 September 2026 says the plant operated at 92 per cent of rated capacity in the week ending 18 September 2026. The record states no customer lead times. On 29 September 2026 Kestrel Semiconductor announced a five-year agreement with TSMC for N3P wafer capacity, 24,000 wafers a month from Q3 2027, plus advanced-packaging slots. The disclosure was made in an exchange filing published before the opening of trading. Kestrel will pay a US$1.1 billion prepayment and gave no margin guidance. The previous contract covered 16,000 wafers a month. On July 25, 2026, Kestrel Semiconductor published its quarterly exchange filings with the Taiwan Stock Exchange and the Tokyo Stock Exchange. The filings, dated July 24, 2026, cover the period from April 1 to June 30, 2026. Kestrel reported net revenue of NT$142.3 billion for the quarter, a figure that appears in the consolidated income statement on page 12 of the Taiwan filing. The company also disclosed a gross margin of 48.7 percent, down from 51.2 percent in the same quarter of 2025. Operating income was NT$38.9 billion, and net income was NT$31.4 billion. These figures are stated in the filing without adjustment for foreign exchange fluctuations. Kestrel's Q3 2026 output filing, submitted to the Malaysian Investment Development Authority on 12 September 2026, reports 38,400 units shipped for the quarter across both plants. The filing attributes 21,600 units to Phase 1 and 16,800 units to Phase 2. Phase 2 output is recorded from 15 August 2026 onward. The company lists no export destinations in the filing. I spent most of the week before the September meeting staring at the same question every rates strategist was asking: how much of this was already in the curve? My honest answer, as of the close on 17 September 2026, was most of it. The hike was roughly 85% priced by 17 September 2026, so the 9 bp rise in the 10-year yield on 18 September 2026 reflects guidance, not the move itself. That distinction matters more than the headline number, and it is the thing I want to unpack here. The yen's recent move is a reminder that currency markets can turn quickly, especially when they are positioned one way. The rate differential remains the dominant driver, but it is not the only one. I will be watching the data, the rhetoric from the BoJ and the Fed, and the positioning of carry traders. As always, I will try to separate what is said and what gets done. That distinction has served me well in the past, and I suspect it will continue to do so. This round allocated a little over 600 MW of new capacity across roughly two dozen buyers. Most contracts run for 21 years, which matches the economic life the developers assume for their panels. The buyers are a predictable mix: data-centre operators in Johor, two glove makers, a brewery, several electronics plants in Kulim and Perak, and one cement works that I suspect signed mainly for the press coverage. When I first started modelling grid load for Southeast Asian data centres, Johor was barely a blip on the radar. That changed around 2022, when Singapore’s moratorium on new data-centre construction pushed operators across the causeway. By early 2026, the scale of announced projects in Johor is staggering. I'll walk through the arithmetic of what this means for the grid by 2030, using primary data from Malaysia’s Energy Commission and my own load models.
